pr_title: Spatial search functions support multi-valued fields in compute engine
pr_body:
In #110830 it was noted that ES|QL produces different results during spatial search for multi-values when we pushdown to lucene versus when we do not. The lucene query understands spatial multi-values, while the compute engine does not.

Normally ES|QL predicates do not support multi-values because it is ambiguous whether the predicate means `ANY` or `ALL` on the multi-value. For example, if the field `age=[10,30]` and we have the query `FROM index | WHERE age > 20`, it should pass for `ANY` and fail for `ALL`. But in order to answer that, the predicate needs knowledge of this choice between `ANY` and `ALL`.

It turns out that this choice is already made for the spatial predicates. They contain knowledge of how to deal with multi-value fields (the choice of `ANY`, `ALL` or some other logic). This is because the spatial types understand the concept of a collection, and already deal with collections, so multi-valued types can be handled naturally. The lucene queries used for lucene-pushdown already support multi-values for spatial predicates like `ST_INTERSECTS`. However, the compute engine does not. The code generated from the `Evaluator` methods explicitly filters out multi-valued fields.

While this PR originally added generic support for multi-value fields using an extension to the `@Evaluator` annotation to explicitly define a combiner (Any vs All combiners), that solution was only sufficient for `ST_INTERSECTS` and `ST_DISJOINT`. It turns out that if the right-hand-side is also compound, then `ST_CONTAINS` and `ST_WITHIN` need more complex support to consider that each of the components of the other parameter needs to be contained or within at least one of the components of the first parameter. For this scenario, it is much simpler to just combined all multi-values into a single parameter before evaluation. For this reason the `@Evaluator` extension was removed in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/112063/commits/1792442e7338a628b2634b5132815158d6ccb692.

Instead the solution chosen here was to pass in the parameters as the original Blocks, and rely on the spatial functions to decide how to deal with them (by merging them into single compound geometries before performing the spatial relationship check). The total code complexity is lower. However, if there is interest in supporting the more general Any/All approach to other predicate functions, then reverting the above mentioned commit is one place to consider starting.

Fixes #110830
Fixed #112102
Fixes #112505
pr_comments: Hi @craigtaverner, I've created a changelog YAML for you.

> `ST_INTERSECTS(field, polygon)` - `true` if `ANY` value can intersect the polygon

What if the RHS is many polygons? Is that true if any field intersects any of the polygons?

> ST_INTERSECTS(field, polygon) - true if ANY value can intersect the polygon
> What if the RHS is many polygons? Is that true if any field intersects any of the polygons?

Yes, intersects is true if the geometries have at least one point in common.

> Yes, intersects is true if the geometries have at least one point in common.

:+1:

And that's what I saw when I reviewed the compute side. Thanks for confirming that's what it's supposed to do.

review_comments: I wonder if this abstraction is really needed. The methods in this class can be implemented as helper methods in SpatialRelatesFunction class?

It is possible, but makes the code more complex. We have 4 methods that take the interface type `MultiValuesCombiner`), and these would need to be doubled to 8 methods (for LongBlock and BytesRefBlock versions) and each would need to add additional position parameters. I think the added complexity is not worth it.
Why don't we use this approach for Intersects and Contains? I would rather prefer to use the same approacch in all functions and it will remove lots of complexity too.
All functions now use the Block.Builder approach.
